utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. -- good morning. Mr. Stamp, I understand you have a matter to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The next witness is Ms. Nazalie Bala in relation to the allegations regarding Pristina events. However, Your Honour, due to scheduling difficulties she will be the only witness we have available today because of the late arrival of some witnesses. I -- it might well be that she may use up the entire day because she is scheduled to be one hour in chief; however, it is possible that there might be a part of the day when we have -- don't have a witness to follow her. Her evidence will be taken by Mr. Eliott Behar. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will see how the day progresses. The witness could be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now please sit down. Mr. Behar has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Bala. Can you please state your full name and date of birth for the record.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Nazalie Bala. I was born on the 17th of May, 1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, I understand that in 1989 you began working in human rights employed as a field researcher for the Council For Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms in Pristina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. From 1989 to 1997 I worked as a researcher, field researcher, for human rights, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And I also understand that in November of 1998 you began working for the OSCE, the Organisation For Security and Cooperation in Europe, also in human rights?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what kind of work you're currently doing?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Presently I work as a project manager in the United Nations development organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And I also understand that you have a master's degree in international diplomacy and relations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, I have an MA in international relations and diplomacy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Bala, do you recall providing a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 30th of June, 2001?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I understand that you also provided an addendum to that statement on the 16th of August, 2006; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to read that statement and that addendum before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And are you satisfied that the information contained in those documents is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender that statement and the addendum that's 65 ter number 02262, and that -- I can indicate that the statement and the addendum are included together in that same package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00420, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, did you testify at the Milutinovic trial on the 22nd and 23rd of August, 2006?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, I was invited as a witness in the Milutinovic trial, and I gave a statement for that trial as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And have you also had a chance to review the transcript of your testimony in that trial?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Does that transcript accurately reflect your evidence and would you testify to the same facts today?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I would testify the same things today, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender 65 ter 05188, the transcript of the witness's testimony from Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00421, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I would just ask if the usher could please provide the witness with a copy of her statement. We'll be referring to it in court. While that's being done I can provide a brief summary of Ms. Bala's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I can indicate, Your Honours, that Ms. Bala's evidence will relate to paragraph 72(g), 73, and 77 of the indictment, and I will provide that summary now. Ms. Bala is a Kosovar Albanian who resided in Pristina. Beginning on the 24th of March, 1999, she made a number of observations of Pristina and the neighbourhoods surrounding her from the roof of her building. She observed that on the 26th of March, 1999, all roads leading in and out of Pristina were blocked; and VJ, MUP, and Serb civilians were manning barbed wire blockades. Overnight in the following days Serb forces and civilians started destroying Albanian houses and shops, forcing people out of their homes, and firing on civilians. There were 100 people seeking refuge in her house by the time she was forced to leave on the 29th of March, 1999. She was made to leave her house and join a convoy of people in the thousands walking to the centre of Pristina. The roads were lined with Serb forces and civilians who had their guns pointed at the convoy. They separated the men from the group and robbed them. The convoy went to the train station and was surrounded there by police. Ms. Bala boarded an overcrowded train that headed in the direction of Kosovo Polje. As the train travelled, the track was lined with VJ and MUP pointing their weapons at the train and yelling ethnic insults. When they arrived at the border in Djeneral Jankovic, they were all told to get off the train and walk towards Macedonia and to walk in the middle of the railway tracks because there were mines on either side. She was eventually placed on a bus going in the direction of Ohrid, Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel kindly slow down while reading, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, I will have a few questions for you in order to clarify certain matters. You describe in your statement, and this is on page 2 of the statement, in the last paragraph on that page that the 24th and 25th of March, 1999, was when NATO commenced bombing Kosovo, including Pristina; and you explain that there were 25 people in your house that night and that by the time you left, several days later, there were about 100 people in your house. Can you explain to us who those people were and how they came to be at your house?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Starting from the 20th of March, 1999, to 29th of March, 1999, I was in Prishtina. Because of the nature of my work, I was used to observing what was happening, so I visited several parts of Prishtina where we were in a very rigid siege by the Serb forces, both police and army forces. In the beginning, there were about 25 members -- family members in my house, while when we left there were about a hundred of us that left together. In the beginning we were just the family, members of my family with whom I lived all my life, while later on relatives came from villages around Prishtina because they were expelled from their homes, and they were afraid of the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us where these homes were that people were coming from.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: These people lived in Dragodan, Vranjevc, Kolovica, the hospital neighbourhood, Sofali, and Taslixhe, these are all areas around Prishtina or in Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And how is it that they ended up coming to your house and, if you know, how did they get to your house?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Well, how they came to my house, this would be a very direct answer: They came to my house because of the bombing, of the repression, of the shelling, the looting, and the killings committed by the Serb forces, both police and military because I don't think those people would like to leave their houses, they just were forced to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'd like to ask as well about some of the direct observations that you described making in Pristina over this time-period. You describe making a number of observations from the top-storey terrace of your house. Can you describe where your house was located in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: My house is still in the same part of Prishtina, in the old town, close to the market. It is a house from where you can see the whole of the town, the Vranjevc hill. You can see Dragodan from there, new Kolovica, and in the part behind the house you can see Taslixhe. It's a two-storey -- it's a five-storey house. There is a cellar and there are storeys above the ground. The house does not have a roof. It is a terraced roof, it's flat, so I could go there and observe all the parts of Prishtina that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can the usher please bring up 65 ter number 00013. And as well, if the witness could be provided with a pen so she can make some markings on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: In your statement you make reference to observations of Dragodan, Vranjevc, Kolovica, Taslixhe. Are you able to indicate what directions those would be on the map and mark them as well -- in fact, I'll just stop you. Before we do that perhaps you can first mark the location of your house on the map.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Can you please zoom it in a little bit because I don't have my glasses with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we can just zoom in more on the top part, if possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My house is about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And as I was starting to mention earlier, can you indicate where on that map - and I know that these places may not directly be on the map - but if you can indicate what directions Dragodan, Vranjevc, Kolovica, and Taslixhe would be.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Dragodan is here, together with a cemetery which links Dragodan and Vranjevc. Vranjevc is here --

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Are you able to write Vranjevc as well.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Kolovica is here, Taslixhe is here, and a small neighbourhood here which is called Sofali.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us what the terrain was like around your house and the surrounding areas. What I mean by that was, Was this a flat area or were any of the areas elevated by hills and valleys?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: The part where my house is is not mountainous, it's a flat area; however, you can see very well towards the north-east, west, and south, because these areas are easily seen from my house. From my house you could see straight to the Vranjevc hill, Dragodan hill, and Taslixhe area. Visibility was really good around the house. For me it was impossible to observe what was happening inside the town, in the centre, because of the buildings. It's a built-up area and there are tall buildings that did not allow me to see what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand from your statement that you were also able to use night-vision goggles. Can you explain how you ended up obtaining night-vision goggles.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: When the OSCE mission left Kosova, the international staff were allowed to take only 20 kilogrammes in their luggage. Myself and many of my colleagues took some of their belongings in our homes. At that time I took my boss to the office of OSCE in Dragodan, behind the American office. There were things there in her luggage and her luggage was in my -- in the boot of my car. The binoculars, the night-vision binoculars were in her luggage, and they were in my possession at the time when she left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. With respect to the events of the 26th of March, 1999, you describe in your statement - and this is on page 3 in the first paragraph - that you observed the roads in and out of Pristina were blocked by blockades and that the Albanians were denied any movement. Can you tell us who was manning those blockades?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I also mentioned earlier that it was a siege. Every point of entrance and exit to Prishtina was blocked. All the crossroads as well were encircled by the police and the army, the Serbian police and army. The parts of Prishtina that linked the outskirts with the centre were also encircled by the Serb military and police forces. So they had under control everything, every movement in Prishtina. I saw this personally because I travelled by car from one place to another in Prishtina, and sometimes I also walked to different places in order to see what was going on inside Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So again, just very briefly and to be clear, who was manning the blockades then that you saw?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: The police, the Serbian police; the Serb army; Serbian civilians, half uniformed, some of them had police jackets and civilian trousers; paramilitaries who were wearing uniforms that I saw for the first time then. They had bandannas on their heads, they had painted faces, different tattoos on their bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement as well - this is in the third paragraph at page 3 - you describe that a man named Latif Sulejmani explained getting to you by crossing three check-points. Can I ask: Did you observe those check-points yourself?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, I saw the check-points myself because I worked in Dragodan, I worked in RC Prishtina, which is behind former American office. The check-point was right at the American office; the second check-point was at the Dragodan bridge; the third one was in Tophane, which links the old part and the new part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Could you mark that on the map, please, and perhaps next to each one you could put the number you've referred to.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: The first check-point was here, the second was here at the bridge, the third one somewhere here, which links the new part and the old parts of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would now seek to tender that map into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00422, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: With respect then, Ms. Bala, to the events of the 29th of March, 1999, you describe in your statement at page 4 that a VJ officer and a gypsy came to your house and told all of you to leave within five minutes. You also explain that those two Serbs would be followed up or those two people would be followed up by a group of mobilised personnel who would beat or kill anyone remaining in the house. Can you explain to us how you knew that or why you say that?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: That afternoon, it was around 4.00 or 5.00 p.m., two people came to our door. They ordered us to leave the house in five minutes, and we went outside. We joined the convoy of people that was in the street, and, meanwhile, another group came to see where the people -- see whether the people had left their houses or not. Those who had not left their houses were beaten and ill treated and even killed. A neighbour of mine who was about 70 years old and his wife, they both refused to leave the house. We were in the neighbourhood. It was a large group of people, a large convoy trying to leave, and the Serb forces came and they began to beat them up. You could hear the 70-year-old man screaming, and we were in the street, and we were not able to go and help them; but we could hear, Please don't, please stop. We could hear that. Later on we continued, and we could not learn what happened to our neighbours. We met them in Ohrid later on, but this man died because of what he had suffered at their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us who were in this second group of personnel? In other words, whether -- who was it made up of? Did you recognise any of the people or any of the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: One of them was my neighbour. He used to work as a traffic policeman. His name was Ivica. He lived just two neighbourhoods away from the part where I lived. However, the other persons forming the second group were not familiar to me. I didn't know any other of them. They would go into two groups. The first group would order people to leave their houses, and the second group would carry out the verification. They would check whether the people left or stayed. If they found someone who refused to leave, who was still in his or her house, then they would exercise brutality on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And were people in the second group of personnel that you described wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: The personnel from the second group was dressed in uniforms, military, police uniforms. There were people who had been mobilised but also who were wearing civilian clothes. So it was a mixed group. They were scattered in different parts of the neighbourhood. For example, they would come as a group as far as the beginning of the neighbourhood. Once they reached the neighbourhood, they will go in smaller groups to check the houses, whether people had left or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. You also explain in the next paragraph that you left your house and you joined a large group of people walking towards the centre of Pristina. Can you describe this group; in other words, how many people were walking on the streets?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: As I said earlier, when we left our houses we were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- when we left the house, we were about 100 people. Once on the street we saw our neighbours who were more or less in the same numbers, in the same situation. They also had people who had come from different parts of Prishtina and the surrounding villages to their houses, who had fled from those areas and sought shelter in their houses. Thousands and thousands of Albanians were walking on the main streets, and they were directed by them to go to the main station in Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Now, you've said "them." Can you explain who "them" was, who was directing you to the centre?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: When I say "them," it always refers to the Serb forces. This is how we identified them. When we refer to the Serb forces, that is, police, army, paramilitaries, and mobilised Serbs, and those who had joined the police and Serb forces. While we were walking along the Prishtina roads, on both sides of the road, we were escorted by the Serb police and army. They had their weapons directed at the population. We were under strict control. We dared not to look on the sides or behind or in front to see what was going on with the other part of the convoy. In the front part of the convoy - and this was a long, long convoy - you could see how people were separated from their families and taken away from the convoy, you could see how people were being looted and beaten there on the streets. Just a detail that I will never forgot as long as I live: A handicapped person, an old man who was being pushed in a wheelchair - I don't remember now exactly whether it was a policeman or a soldier - ordered his son to leave the wheelchair behind, to leave his father or grandfather, the disabled person, behind and to proceed without him. We passed that part where they ordered this young man to leave the wheelchair behind, and about 10 metres further we just heard a gun-shot. There was no movement or scream afterwards. We couldn't know what happened to that disabled person. We just had to proceed in the direction of the station. In addition to the main forces who controlled our movements, there was pressure from the civilian Serb population that had come out on the streets, on both sides of the streets, and on their balconies because we were walking along an area that had buildings on both sides. They would throw different things on us such as vases, bottles, metal items; and they were shouting at us and at the forces telling them, Kill them all. Let them remember what happened in Bosnia. Let them know what Serbia is. Let them know whose Kosova is. And used offensive language at us. So this is how we were escorted up to the train station, under strict control by the Serb police and army forces, and by the damages and offences suffered from the civilian population, Serb civilian population. And the police didn't even stop them in throwing things from their balconies, didn't even tell them that that was not something good to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You also describe in your statement arriving at the railway station at noon, and you described there being thousands of people waiting to get on the train. You also describe being surrounded by police who you recognised as police from the Dragodan region. How did you know that they were from Dragodan?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I knew they were policemen from Dragodan because my office was at Dragodan. It was called RC, regional centre, Prishtina at the time. So every second or third day on the way to or from the office it was impossible to pass without being stopped at the check-point by the policemen. They were carrying out their role as traffic policemen at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Now, you describe in your statement the train arriving at the station, and you described there being about 30 passenger cars attached to the engine. Can you tell us, was anyone guarding the train?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: When we arrived at the train station, it seemed to me as if the entire population of Prishtina was there, children, youth, women, elderly, tired, scared, traumatised, exhausted, people who had spent even a night there at the train station. We joined this crowd of people and waited until they brought the train at around 5.00 p.m., as far as I remember. It was a train consisting of about 30 passenger cars. The rear part --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the part behind the train was a hilly part, and there was a large group of policemen who were observing the flat part; and the part behind us was also under the control of the Serb police forces. We were ordered to board the train, to get on the train. You can imagine how big is the space or how small, rather, is the space in the passenger cars. We were forced to actually put our children in the compartments for the luggage because there was no space in there. We were about 50 persons per carriage, and even today we -- when we speak with people about this we cannot help it but surprise -- get surprised how they could put all of us in such a small space where none of us could move left or right. The doors and the windows of the train were shut, and this is how the train proceeded its route to Fushe Kosove.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a couple of questions to clarify. You mentioned 50 persons per carriage, that's how it was interpreted. Can you explain what you mean by "carriage," where the 50 persons were that you described.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Compartment, maybe it's a language issue, difference between Albanian and English. One compartment can have one or two -- one carriage can have one or two compartments. I'm speaking about one compartment where about 50 persons were placed, not a carriage. Maybe a carriage at the time could take about 200 people. There were also corridors that were full. There were children also in those parts of corridors where you can put your luggage. It was impossible to -- for the adults to keep or hold their children with them because it was very difficult to breathe in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If I could have Exhibit 00001, that's the Times map of the western Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Bala, while we're waiting for the map, I can indicate that I'm just going to ask you if you can indicate the route that your train took on this map. And perhaps after each place that you mention, you can stop; and I may have a question or two before we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we could just have that zoomed in on the area between Pristina and the Macedonia border. Perhaps just higher up as well if possible. That's great. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So we know that you left from Pristina. Can you indicate where you went from there?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: This is Prishtina, and from here the train travelled in the direction of Fushe Kosove, where it stopped, from Prishtina to Fushe Kosove. During this part of the journey, especially when we entered Fushe Kosove, we saw houses that had been burnt and destroyed. In Fushe Kosove we saw bodies that had been burnt or half burnt, people that had been killed and their bodies lying there on the streets. At Fushe Kosove the train stopped, and we were faced with horror. We were scared. People with masks, without masks, with painted faces, police forces, military forces, mobilised people, civilians, all of them armed with their guns directed at us on both sides, meaning from the right and from the left of the train. The children were crying and screaming in the train. They were not aware of what was going on. From outside we were threatened by them. They would say that if they hear a single cry, a single scream from the children they will come up in the train and kill us. They would say they were going to execute us, that they would take us to a factory, to another place, and that they will suffer an even worse fate than that of the Bosnians in Srebrenica. Then the train proceeded to Lipjan from Fushe Kosove --

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Okay, sorry, I'll just stop you there. So the train -- and we may need to go through just a little more quickly as we're somewhat short of time. If you can indicate then where the train went from there and simply whether or not it stopped at the next location.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: From Fushe Kosove the train proceeded to Lipjan; from there to Ferizaj; and from Ferizaj to Hani i Elezet, or the border with Macedonia, that is near the cement factory at Hani i Elezet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender that map as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00423, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: In your statement - and this is on the fourth page in the second paragraph, you describe that the train arrived in front of a cement factory at Hani i Elezet at about 8.00 p.m., and you clarify in your addendum that that was at 10.00 p.m. Can you tell us what happened after you were told to get off the train?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: After we arrived at Hani i Elezet near this cement factory, the train stopped. We were encircled by the Serb forces, that is, there were Serb police and military forces on both sides of the train with their guns directed at the Albanian population on the train. We were immediately told to get off the train, all of us, and they then asked us to provide them with our ID cards. Myself and my family were in the front part of the train, maybe in the third or fourth compartment. So when they told us to produce our IDs, I saw that they realised that there were far too many people, and they stopped asking for these IDs. I could see the first group of them who asked for the ID cards. And as soon as they had the ID cards in their hands they would tear them and throw them away. When I would look back just to see how many of us were there, I could also see how people, mainly men, were separated from their families. I saw cases of looting when they took away everything that the civilian population had on them. Personally I can speak of my own family. We didn't have anything on us except for a bottle for the 2-year-old because we were not allowed to take anything with us. So when we left, not even clothes for the children. They would take away everything -- anything they could find on you. They then told us to form a line of two. They told us to walk on the rails -- on the tracks and proceed towards Macedonia. When we were told to form this line of two, they told us not to leave the tracks because both sides were mined. This is how we walked towards Macedonia, on rail tracks and in a minefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You then describe arriving at the grain yard, in other words, at the end of your walk. Did you meet or speak with other people once you were there?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: There were other people there at the meadow, at that field in Blace; people who had been waiting for a week to cross the border with Macedonia; people who had previously gone through looting, beating, horror; people who had been stripped of everything they had, vehicles, money, valuables, personal belongings, and who had been forced to leave their homes and cross the border to Macedonia; people who had spent almost a week in the no man's land between Macedonia and Kosovo. Not only those who arrived there on train, but people who had arrived there from the area near the border, Kacanik and Ferizaj area, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And can you tell us where you went from the border?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: When we arrived at the border, which we called Blace, a week -- approximately a week later, a humanitarian catastrophe began known to the whole world. In the beginning we were told that we would be taken to Ohrid --

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I'll just stop you before we continue. I want to be careful about going into too much hearsay, but if you can just describe very briefly where you went once you left the border region and how you got there.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: From the border we went to Gostivar, to Negotin village in Gostivar area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And Gostivar, I understand it -- I see the map that is up as well, am I correct that that's in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, that's in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I don't need you to mark it at this time. Can you tell us what was your status in Macedonia when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: A status of a refugee as all others.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bala. Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Behar. Mr. Djurdjic, do you have cross-examination? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Bala, my name is Veljko Djurdjic. I'm a member of the Djordjevic Defence team. My associate, Marie O'Leary, is assisting me today; she's a member of our team. Mr. Dragoljub Djordjevic is away today because he is busy preparing our Defence case. I have a number of questions for you, Madam. First of all, there's something that I have observed in your evidence today. There are a number of things that you never said before. The first thing is about you personally going to a number of check-points that you saw in town. When you were on your way to work in Dragodan they stopped you because that's where your office was. Can you please tell us why you never stated this before. You have provided a number of statements, in 1999, in 2001, in 2006, and then in the Milutinovic trial. Why have you never stated this before, Madam?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: The question was asked here whether I knew these policemen, which area they were from, and my answer was I knew these policemen because when I worked for the OSCE, when I walked or went through that area, especially at the Dragodan bridge, we were stopped and we were asked to produce our IDs and licence. Before I was not asked that question. Today that question was asked of me, and I answered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So far you've been saying that you were told this by some other people, yet today you are presenting this to us as your own personal experience.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: If you read my statement more carefully, you will see that there are two explanations. The first one is about before the 26th of March, where the Sulejmani family, Latif and Nexhmedin Sulejmani came to my house and told us what was going on in Dragodan and who had stopped them where. While in the statement I made today and in my testimony today, I explained how I was stopped by these policemen. And the question was asked of me, How did you know -- or did I know these policemen. And I said that, yes, I had seen them before. These were policemen who had been working in that area. And one other small detail: The police command in Prishtina was divided into separate areas. The Dragodan, the Germi, the Vranjevc, and other areas. And the Dragodan area was under the control of the Dragodan police. The Vranjevc area where the police station is still there today was controlled by those forces there --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Bala. That's not what my question was about. Could you perhaps please tell me, since you know those two police officers, what their names were?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I gave just one name, Ivica. This was a traffic policeman. I did not give the name of the other policeman. Ivica was together with a group of other police when they forced us out of our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Madam, I'm asking you about the two policemen you knew who worked in Dragodan, the ones you mentioned for the very first time today, near your own work-place. I see five, that's where it was. I'm asking you about those two policemen, and we'll be returning to Ivica later on.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I don't know the names of the policemen in Dragodan. I know them by their appearance. If I see them today I could point them out, yes, but their names I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have never before used the term "paramilitary" in any of your statements. This is the very first time you've used it. What exactly do you mean when you say "paramilitary," please?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: It's not true that I have not mentioned that earlier. If you read my statement, it has been used several times. This is -- by "paramilitaries," I mean non-regular forces. I've seen regular army before and I had seen them even as a child. I know what they are. The paramilitary forces in Prishtina were numerous, people in uniform, dark or black uniforms, their emblems were not army emblems, with flags that had skulls and a cross on the skulls. Then these were people that had painted faces, beards, long hair, with very irregular appearance which is not suitable for a regular military formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, today is the first time you mention those persons wearing masks and also persons with their face painted. I've read carefully through all of your statements, and I've never come across these references before. Never mind. Let us please move on. Ms. Bala, you talk about Lapi, Street number 30, Pristina, that route?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. If you could clarify it, please, for me. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, Is it true that your family home in Pristina is at Lapi Street number 30 in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: No, that's, that's wrong. It's a mistake. I don't know where you got this information, Ulpiana street. My address is Llapi Street, number 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I never mentioned Ulpiana Street. I look at the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There seems to be some possible interpretation problem or a misspeaking. Will you please repeat your original question to which you want an answer, please, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was about Lapi Street, number 30, in Pristina. Was their family home always there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And your answer, please, Ms. Bala.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the NATO bombing and the beginning of the war, we lived in Triglav street. Today it's called Enver Berisha Street. In the beginning of January 1998, we moved into number 30, Llapi Street, and we still live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter document 00013, can we please have that brought up on our screens. Thank you. My associate tells me this is P422, yes, that's MFI'd and the one that I need is P00013, which is unmarked. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, could you please use this map and mark the location of your house. We have a new unmarked map now.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: This is not a map containing all the streets, so I will only be approximate here. My house is about here, because the green market is very close to where I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please mark the railway station.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, approximately. Just a second, please. Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There's something I'd like to ask you. What about Lapi Street, was it once called Sejdo Bajramovic Street?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: No, never. Llapi street was never Sejdo Bajramovic Street, it was always Llapi Street, while the Triglav Street that I mentioned earlier and later after the independence of Kosovo, the Triglav Street was called Sejdo Bajramovic. The Llapi road has never been called that, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you mark the house, please, or rather, where you marked your present home could you put a 1 there, please.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Right here in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Number 2 next to the railway station. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the previous house in which you lived before you moved to this new location, where was that one?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Put a number 3 there, please.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who were you living with in this new house in 1999?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: With my parents, two brothers, their wives, their children, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What age were your brothers?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: My oldest brother is now 50, second brother is 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What exactly did they do for a living back in 1999?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: The eldest brother was a taxi-driver, the second brother worked as a driver with the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was your father working at the time too?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: No, he had retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did he retire?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: In 1990/1991, that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he receiving his pension?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Until December 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you not know that in 1999 and throughout the war all of the retired people in Pristina continued to receive their pensions?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I would be curious to know where did you get the addresses to send the pensions to because the pensioners were in Albania, in Macedonia, or in the mountains. Where did you send them to? I would be curious to know. Yes, the pensions were paid to the Serbs, to the Bosnians, and the Roma who were living in Kosova at the time, but not to the Albanians. There were over a million people who were expelled, who were in refugee camps. I don't know if you have any information about addresses where these pensions were sent to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. If you'd been listening to my questions more closely you would have heard me suggest that I was talking about those in Pristina who had registered addresses there, they were receiving their pensions. I don't believe your father necessarily informed any state bodies about his whereabouts. And what about the war, were any remaining and still outstanding salaries eventually paid to him?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Not only my father, but no other pensioner, Albanian pensioner, in Kosova received their pensions after December 1998. The pensioners' fund that existed before 1998 and after that, it was kept in Serbia. It was not given to people, to the Albanian people in Kosova. The Serbs, the Bosnians, and the Roma in Pristina and in other places did receive their pensions, but I asked you earlier and my question is -- still is: Where did you get the addresses for people who were expelled from Kosova? Where did you send those pensions to? There was internal displacement. People were also expelled outside the country and you're speaking about their pensions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, you have a degree in economics. Where was that degree obtained, which university?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I gratitude two faculties, the faculty of economy in Prishtina, and I also did political studies. I specialised in Tirana in diplomacy, and I earned my MA in international relations and diplomacy in 2006. From 1999 until today I also have attended many training courses in various parts of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to know, first of all, about your degree in economics. Was that degree obtained at the Pristina University, the state universe, or a different school of economics?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I received my diploma in -- from the University of Prishtina. There is just one university in Prishtina and it is still functioning today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was a state-owned university, right? When you obtained your degree?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I can see that you want more explanation, and I will give those explanations if you are willing to hear me out. In 1992 all the secondary schools and the Prishtina University were -- closed their doors to Albanians. Albanians were not allowed to attend those schools. From 1992 till after the war, the education and training of people was done in an alternative form. We tried to keep education alive for children and students. My diploma is from the University of the Republic of Kosova, that's what we called it then, and many other people like me received their diplomas there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you get your degree recognised domestically in any official, formal way?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, it is recognised in my country, not only my diploma but the diplomas of all those students and people who graduated before 1998 in extraordinary circumstances. All those diplomas are recognised. There are people who went on to study for their Ph.D.s in various European universities based on the diploma they had received in their own country.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you because you say you obtained a diploma and still you couldn't get a job. Well, how could you possibly expect to get a job if you had a degree from a university that was not officially recognised?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: After what happened with the education system in Kosova, and I know about this because I was collecting information and facts about what happened in Kosova at the time, all the Albanians who were working in that system were expelled from their jobs in 1999 -- 1992. So it was not logical for me to ask for -- to go and ask for a job in those structures anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, there were courses in two languages at the state university, both Serbian and Albanian. Can you please tell me what year you enrolled?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: The state university which was founded in 1974, if I remember correctly, it is true that courses were held in Albanian and Serbian then. This continued up until 1992. In 1992 no educational establishment in Kosova that was called a state educational establishment was -- held their courses in Albanian. Everything was in Serbian. That's why we established the parallel system of education, to educate our students and pupils, and this was the parallel system.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But my question was about your year of enrolment, in which university?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: 1987. I enrolled ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, there is a misunderstanding, it appears. Which year did you enroll in the faculty of economics and which faculty university was that, a state university or not?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I don't know how relevant this is to my statement. Is it necessary for me to answer this question because I don't see how it is related to what I have stated in my statement. I enrolled in 1987. At that time, the courses were held in both languages, Albanian and Serbo-Croatian. I began my studies and then the situation deteriorated, and I started work in the Council for the Defence of Human Rights. And later on, I continued my studies in the parallel education system, so I only studied for a year in the Prishtina state university; later on, I continued my studies in the parallel system.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just another question. At the time after you had enrolled, did you become a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I don't know which system you come from, but as you may know in 1987 there was just one political party, the communist league, and all other parties, pluralism, emerged later on. So you may well know that there was no other party at that time, in 1987. It was a one-party system, so I really don't know which other parties you are referring to that existed at the time. As I already told you, there was only one party, the communist league then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this might be a good time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We still have on our screens the map, Mr. Djurdjic. Are you planning to tender that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour. I will be going through the witness's statement, and I kept the map because I wanted her to mark some more locations for us so we might have a map that we can use for all these different reference points, in order to avoid having to pull them up again. I thought we should just press on with this one. If you think it's technically more convenient to have this one admitted now and then bring up a new blank map to mark further locations, I'm ready to be so instructed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The problem is a technical one, Mr. Djurdjic. Over the break we are likely to lose this if it is not saved and exhibited at this point. Before we do receive it, though, Ms. Bala, would you be able to look back to the map on your screen. You were asked to mark with a number 2 the position of the railway station, and you marked a position you said you thought it was in that area. Is that your understanding that you marked the railway station as best you could?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since this is a map that does not contain the names of the streets in details, I did my best to mark the approximate area. It should be somewhere in this area that I marked or in this area that I just marked. As I said, there were no details -- this is not a detailed map. Even the house, my house that I marked, is an approximate area. Maps tend to change. There are maps with more details, but unfortunately this one doesn't have those details. Had these details been there, I would have been able to mark the exact location of the train station. I passed by that location every day to carry out my normal, daily activities. Therefore, the markings that I made are approximate, not exact because of the reasons that I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The reason I asked is because well over on the left-hand side of the map there appears to be marked a railway line, and a little below the centre of the map well on the left-hand side there appears to be some two or three sets of parallel tracks, whereas there appears to be no railway line marked in the area where you have marked the railway station. Now, it may be that something is not shown on the map or it may be that you were not correctly oriented when you marked the railway station. Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are fully right, Your Honour. As I said earlier, it is quite difficult to orient myself on this map. You are completely right. The train station should be somewhere here, and I apologise for this misreading of the map. But as I said, I passed by that train station on a daily basis to carry out my normal, daily activities. I apologise once again. You're fully right. This road here goes to Fushe Kosove, and it's behind the Grand Hotel in Rilindija building and other well-known buildings in the centre of Kosova. I apologise once again, Your Honour, for not marking correctly the location of the train station at the outset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: To help us to follow your markings in the future, would you please put a number 4 with the marking which you now say is the railway station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not 100 per cent sure, and I cannot pin-point the exact location; so I would like to stress once again that this is the approximate area. I'll mark it with a 4. The map is such that it is difficult for me to identify the exact locations. It's a small building compared to the building in Fushe Kosove, the building of the train station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I think counsel have followed that. After the break, Mr. Djurdjic, if you need to follow that up further, you can. We will receive the map as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00050, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, we must now have the first break so that the tapes can be rewound, and that means we will resume at ten minutes past 11.00. The court staff will assist you outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Madam Bala, were you a member of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: No, never in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you from 1990 when the multi-party system was introduced were a member of any political party; and if so, which political party, please?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: In 1989 I began to work as an activist for human rights in the Council of the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms in Kosova. I was and I still am a regular activist of this council. Later on I joined the Democratic League of Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that the party which was headed by Mr. Ibrahim Rugova?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: This political party was all people movement. It was led by Dr. Ibrahim Rugova, now deceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you still a member of the Democratic League of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: No, I'm not a member of the Democratic League of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Are you a member of any other political party; and if so, when did you join?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I will give you a general answer so that I can make your questions shorter. I see that you want to know whether I am a member of the Democratic League of Kosova, led by Hashim Thaqi. After the war new political parties developed and emerged in Kosova. In 2001 I joined the Democratic Party of Kosova, and I was a member of this party until 2007. I could no longer be an active member of this party because of my obligations and work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just ask you: When did you finish your studies of political sciences and where, since you told us that you graduated from political sciences?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Until 2001 I continued my work with the OSCE mission. In 2001 I stopped my employment with them because of the studies and further commitments. Until 2006 I continued and finished my studies at the University of Prishtina at the Faculty of Philosophy. Further on I enrolled a master's programme, a dual programme, an exchange between the Diplomatic Academy in Vienna and the Business College in Kosova. This is a programme that I finished in 2006, or rather, I graduated in 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you told us that you started in 1989 working at a committee for human rights at Pristina. Could you tell us, please, who founded that committee and what were the [indiscernible] goals of that committee?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: The Committee for the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms in Kosova was established on the 10th of December, 1989, by intellectuals or group of activists in the field of protection of human rights and freedoms in Kosova. Initially the committee was led by the well-known activist who was killed during the war, Bajram Kelmendi, and by other intellectuals from Kosova. The council or the committee was also led by Adem Demaqi, who was also an activist in the field of protection of human rights in Kosova. He was imprisoned for 28 years during the times of former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Adem Demaqi the leader or, as you said, Mr. Kelmendi?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Initially when the committee was set up, it was led by the well-known lawyer Bajram Kelmendi. Later on, when the committee was well-established, Adem Demaqi was appointed the leader or the head of the Committee for the Protection of Human Rights in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you sent as a member of that committee abroad to attend some courses?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: As a member of the Committee for the Protection of Human Rights and Freedom, in addition to the courses that we attended inside Kosova in the field of protection of human rights and freedoms, I also attended a similar course in 1996 in an academy of Lillehammer, in Norway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you go to Switzerland to attend some courses there?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: In Geneva, yes, in the UN human rights organisation in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who funded your travels?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: My travels were mainly funded by those who invited us to attend these seminars or training courses, the organisers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you funded by the American Information Centre in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I never attended a training course funded by the information centre -- American Information Centre in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Madam Bala, I asked you whether the American Information Centre at Pristina funded your travels and didn't ask you about the courses.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you leave the Committee of Human Rights and Freedoms; and if so, could you please explain the reasons?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I never left the committee. I'm still a regular or active member of this committee. I established an NGO that dealt with gender issues and violence against women in Kosova. This was a registered NGO at the time, active as early as in 1997. I joined the OSCE in December 1998, but the organisation called Elena based in Prishtina was active at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the name Behxhet Shala mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: It means a lot. He's still a friend of mine. We worked together in the Committee for the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms. He still works there as the executive director of this committee. At the time he was a secretary of the committee, the time that we worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You never had any conflicts with the members of the executive committee and subsequently left, did you?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me, what were the goals of the Committee for the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms? What was their agenda?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: The goals of the committee was to record and collect facts pertaining to the violation of human rights and freedoms in Kosova, collection of facts, information, statement, photographs, compiling weekly, biannual, monthly reports, that were sent to different international organisations who deal with the issue of human rights. These reports were published by different embassies in Belgrade at the time and by different international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that it went for the protection of human rights of all persons irrespective of their ethnic background who lived at Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: The committee collected and recorded facts of violation of human rights. We did not protect the human rights because we were -- there was situations that we could not exercise that task, but it did its work irrespective of the persons and their ethnic groups or gender or race.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me where I can find a report on the kidnapping of Serbs during 1998/1999, about the murder of policemen and troops in 1998/1999, about the kidnapping of Albanians who were loyal to the state, any reports on the kidnapped Serbs from Orahovac in July 1998?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: During 1998/1999 I worked for the OSCE mission in Kosova. As for the reports that you mentioned, you probably know that the humanitarian fund, law fund, is operating; and they probably have all this information that you asked me about in their files, and you can also find this information with the OSCE mission that was active at the time in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But, Madam Bala, in one version of your statements you started on the 4th of January, 1999, working for the OSCE; and now in November 1998. Thank you. What about the period 1994, 1995, 1996, 1997, is there any report on the violation of human rights of non-Albanians that we may find?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I didn't bring any reports with me here, but if you are interested in finding those reports, you can contact the Council for the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please tell us who funded the Committee for the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: From 1989 until 1997, as -- I'm speaking now in capacity of a witness here before this Tribunal, I worked for the council as a volunteer. The council or the committee was funded by different donators, but it didn't have a regular financing that would enable it to function in practice. But despite the difficult conditions and financial problems, we never stopped our work. We would always go out and perform our work on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Bala. But -- and I do not understand the first paragraph of your statement, that in June 2001 the way you stated that you couldn't find a job as an economist, but you gained employment in the Committee for the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I see that you've mixed up the dates. I will repeat and clarify this with you. I began my work with the council in 1989, and I worked there till early 1997. I then established the NGO dealing with the violation of the rights of women, with gender issues. In early 1998 I joined the OSCE verification mission in Kosova, and I remained with the OSCE until 19th of March, 1999. As a refugee in Macedonia, I continued to work with the OSCE mission in the field of protection of human rights in different refugee camps all over Macedonia. Upon my return, 16th or 17th June, 1999, I'm the first local employee that returned with the OSCE mission in Kosova. I continued my work, my employment, with them until June or July 2001, and that's when I stopped my regular employment from 7.00 to 6.00 p.m. because I decided to start my master's programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Bala, you provided me with a lengthy and exhaustive answer, but not to my question. My question was: You state in -- on the 30th of June, 2001, as well as in the 14th of May, 1999, statement that you could not find employment as an economist but you got employed by the Committee for the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms. You started in 1990, but today you stated in 1989. If you stated that you were employed, which means that you received salary, so it was not volunteer work, as you claim today.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: In my testimony the last time I also mentioned that it was voluntary work. All those years of work in the Council for the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms was voluntary work, not only by me but also other people, my colleagues. Just voluntary work. People from the council working all over Kosova were working voluntarily for the council, the -- all 30 branches of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I will have to read part of your statement dated 30th of June, 2001, in which you say: "In 1992 I graduated from school of economy but I could not" -- thank you. I apologise. "However, from 1990 I had started working for the human rights of Kosovar Albanians in Kosovo, and got employed as a field researcher by the Council for Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms in Pristina ..." and then in a note dated 14th April 2000 at Tetovo under paragraph 2 you say: "I worked in the Committee for the Protection of Human Rights, I worked there from 1990 to 1997, and then I was employed with the Council for the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms in Pristina as a field researcher."

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: This is my statement, but I don't understand your question. You are asking whether I was paid monthly by the council. I will repeat again that everything I did for the council, my work was all voluntarily. 50 people worked voluntarily in that council. I joined the council. I worked shifts. One week I would work from 8.00 to 5.00, the other week I would work from 2.00 p.m. to 8.00 p.m. That was regular work I did for the council.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you find the money to survive all those years?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: There was solidarity amongst Albanians, not only myself but over half the population that was active -- that could work was not able to find work because of the total destruction of the economy in Kosova. We were funded by relatives in Switzerland. My brother used to live in Copenhagen and he sent us remittances. So these were the funds we had, and these were enough to get by day-to-day and to enable me to work for this office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Weren't your brother together at the house where you resided in 1999 Pristina, as you stated today here?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: In order to explain this better: We are eight children, five brothers, three sisters, and we have 18 nieces and nephews. It's a very large family, as you can see. Before the war my brother and my sister lived abroad, my sister in Switzerland, my brother in Copenhagen, and I explained in my earlier answer who funded us. My brother at the time was a manager -- a hotel manager in Copenhagen. My third brother who was a refugee with me, he lives in Sydney, Australia, presently, while my eldest brother, my sister, and two other brothers live in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us what were the goals of the centre for the protection of rights of men and women, Elena.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: The goals of this centre were to identify occurrences of violations of human rights of women by various institutions and the violation of children's rights. This was a specialised recording and reporting of these occurrences in conformity with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Freedoms of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who funded your activities?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: The activities of the NGO that I founded were funded by various foreign donors. We had as our main donor the organisation Mama Cash from the Netherlands, another organisation in the United States, however, this did not last for long. The war started and everything was interrupted. Our activity was interrupted because -- for security reasons and because we were not able to travel in various parts of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Bala, did your organisation cooperate with the government of Mr. Bukoshi?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you cooperate with Xhafer Shatri; did you supply him with information?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the KLA, did you supply any information to the KLA on the Albanian non-governmental organisations from Kosovo and Metohija that were working with the authorities of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I never had any contact with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you organise patrols across Kosovo and Metohija comprising members of your female peace groups, the purpose of those patrols being to monitor any activity by the army and the police?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: No, no. Our organisation identified occurrences of violation of rights of women in Kosova; because at that time, regardless of their age, gender, religion, ethnic group, et cetera, people were being killed in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The answer was no. When you answer "no," please don't continue answering, because once you've said no that is quite sufficient. That is an answer to my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I was trying to explain, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Madam, what was it you were trying to explain? I asked whether you were supplying information on any movement by the army or the police, that was my question. If there is anything to add apart from your answer, the answer being no, anything to do with your potential monitoring activity, then please explain. If a no is a simple no, then let's just move on. Ms. Bala, in addition to your own allegations, do we have anything else to prove that you were working for the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Could you explain a bit further? I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In addition to your own allegations that you were working for the OSCE, is there any evidence indicating that? Because if so, we have seen none here so far to corroborate your allegation that you were working with the OSCE at the time you specify, that is, before the war.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: What kind of evidence would you like to have? You can Google my name and you can find information there on the internet -- in the internet, that I have worked with the OSCE before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Likewise, I would like to ask you about the time you left Serbia. I'm talking about the moment you crossed the border to Macedonia; between that point in time and your eventual return, do you have anything to prove that you were working with the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: First of all, I did not leave Serbia. I was expelled from Kosova, which is my country, and again you can ask for information yourself about me. I worked for the OSCE with a verification mission. We worked in the Sanakos camp, in the Cegran camp, Stenkovec 1 and 2 camps, and I worked also in areas where the Albanians were staying in private homes with the Albanians of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, what you have just said is not what you said in June 2001 when you made your statement.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: There is no other statement. I worked for the OSCE before the war, during the war, and after the war; and you can ask for information about this at the human resource office of the OSCE in Prishtina. They have records of the people who have worked for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would I be right to say that the OSCE left Kosovo and Metohija on the 20th of March, 1999, because of the plummeting living standards of the Kosovar Albanians and the cruel treatment of the Serbs in Kosovo of the Albanian community as well as the rising violence rates that were politically motivated?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I think you must know why the verification mission came to Kosova. At that time there was an agreement on stopping the violence from spreading any further; however, the violation of human rights, the brutality, killings, injuries, arrests, these were everyday occurrences in the lives of Albanians. So the Serbs and the Albanians could not reach an agreement amongst themselves to stop this violence and the violence escalated, so the verification mission left in March 1999, 20th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe it was possible to keep this much briefer. I quoted extensively from your statement on the 13th of June, 2001. Is the quote accurate or not? You can just say yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Well, I have to give the gist of it here and then if you ask me to give further information, it would take weeks to explain you everything that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, I used a quote from your own statement. The question was: Is that faithfully reflected, accurately recorded, or not? The answer is a simple yes or no. I did not elicit any further explanations from you. Just tell me about whether what I read out to you is accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, I'm sorry, if you were quoting from the statement it was not apparent to me that that is what you were doing. I don't think you said you were doing it, and it is not clear now from the transcript what is the quotation from the statement. You are asking

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is it correct or not? The Chamber doesn't know what it is. I suspect the witness may not know what it is. If you could ask the witness to direct her attention to a particular passage of the statement and then ask whether it is correct, you might get somewhere which is more useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. You are entirely right. I did say my next question, though, that I had just quoted the June 13th, 2001, statement, but maybe the best thing to do would be to pull it up on our screens, D002-1741 -- or rather, my associate informs me this is P420, Exhibit 420.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you see that, Ms. Bala? You have the English on the right-hand side or would you prefer to have the Albanian? The Albanian is on the left, right? Paragraph 3: [In English] "The living standard of the Kosovo Albanians in Kosovo and the harsh treatment by the Serbs in Kosovo of the Albanian community had deteriorated to an all low and because of the violence being instilled and for the political reasons on the 19th March, 1999, the OSCE prepared to evacuate." [Interpretation] That's the portion. Yes, my question is: Is it accurately recorded, paragraph 3, what it says. Is it true? Is that what you said? I'm not asking anything special apart from that.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct that I said that. We all experienced what I wrote down here, and if you want any further explanation I can give them to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bala. No further explanations are required. The question was simply: Is this an accurate quote? Thank you. I would like to ask you: When do you think your memory was best and clearest of all these events that you are giving evidence about, since you have provided a number of statements over some time?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: What period of time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I've looked at your statements, they appear to be starting on the 14th of April, 1999; and then the 13th of June, 2001; and then 2006, another statement you made; and then you appeared as a witness in the Milutinovic case; today being the last instance.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
