utterances.text: Well, the experiences are indelible, the things I've been through, things that I have seen and experienced. What I have stated about the 20th to the 29th of March, 1999, I still have those events fresh in my memory although almost ten years have passed from that week.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But please, for the sake of expeditiousness, try to keep your answers brief. So you remember very well all these things. A single sentence would have sufficed to say that. Ms. Bala, if I look at the note made on the 14th of April, 1999, the statement you say that the OSCE left Pristina on the 24th of March, 1999, and that they were preparing to evacuate on the 23rd of March; is that true?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I don't know where you are reading from. The OSCE left on the 20th of March. The 24th of March is the date when the NATO bombing started in Serbia and various parts of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Madam, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have D002-1761.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, this note was drawn up by an OTP investigator on the 14th of April, 1999, interviewed you at Tetovo. And if you look at the note, if you look at all the bullets, bullets 5 and 6 specifically, they state exactly what I've read back to you.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: It must be a misinterpretation of dates, nothing more. The OSCE left Kosova in -- on the 20th of March of 1999 and then on the 24th of March NATO bombing started on targets in Kosova and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may this 14th of April, 1999, interview note please be admitted. I shall continue to use it for the purposes of my cross, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it, Ms. Bala, that you were interviewed by somebody in April 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And was that somebody, as you understood it, from this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must have been from the Tribunal; however, to ask for precise dates a week after the traumatising events we went through, it's not a normal situation when the person is distressed. So this is just a confusion of dates, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you see these notes at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you the truth, I can't remember. I must have seen them, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I notice in the heading your present employment was given as OSCE. That was correct at that time, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please make -- give me the reference as to where you see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the headings, the more heavy type at the top of the page, there's a series of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it now, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was that correct at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I will clarify, if you allow me, sir. I was in Macedonia on the 1st of April, in Negotin, and I asked to be able to find an international who worked for the OSCE. I contacted my former colleagues, international colleagues; and from these contacts, I was able to start working two days later and collect data from eye-witnesses for the events that had occurred in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the person who interviewed you at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: These notes then will be received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00051, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps I should have prefaced this by saying that the 13th of June, 2000, statement, paragraph 2, sees the witness confirm a previous interview with an OTP investigator from the ICTY in relation to events that I'm about to describe on the 14th of April, 1999, in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, the note is dated the 14th of April, 1999. You state that on the 24th of March, at 9.00, you drove in a car into town to see what the Serb authorities were doing and to hear the opinion of the local population. The local population was preparing for a Serbian invasion and some had even sent their families away from Pristina. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Before the 24th, when the NATO air-strikes began, not only on the 24th but as of the 20th of March, I went out down-town to see what was going on because we all knew that after the evacuation of the OSCE people, something bad was going to happen. It is true that I did go and tour different parts of Prishtina to see what was going on and talked to many people and collected different information from these people on what was -- what had happened on that particular day. There was this general fear that the Serbs were going to retaliate on the civilian population in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, is it true that certain people sent their families away from Pristina? Because this is something you stated.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, it is true that certain people sent their families away from Prishtina because of fear that something bad was going to happen by these Serb police and military forces. These families lived in the outskirts of Pristina at the time. You can draw similarity with my situation as some family members or relatives came to live with us. These relatives came from the outskirts of Pristina to live with us at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you said they left Pristina, and now you're telling me they came to Pristina. Nevertheless, let's move on. What sort of a telephone line did you have in your home in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: It was land-line, and I also had a private mobile phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would I be right to say that on the 24th of March electricity had been cut off in Pristina but only for the duration of the air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: As soon as the first bombs fell in Prishtina, the electricity was cut off and it remained cut off until later at night. Later on in different parts, not in the whole area of Prishtina, the electricity remained cut off and in some parts there was electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I look at the notes dated the 14th of April, 1999, I don't see any reference to air-strikes or you trying to observe anything at all from your terrace.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Well, we all know that there was -- there were NATO air-strikes on Serb targets, on the 24th of March. When the bombing stopped I went to the terrace to observe. There was no movement of people. There was movement of different military and police vehicles. There was movement of Serb civilians who were firing in the air in different parts of Prishtina. You could hear this very well, and you could see this very well too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Behar, you -- there's a matter you wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, just that my friend, counsel for Mr. Djordjevic, mentioned that there was no mention of air-strikes, but in fact on that document, I think it's about nine bullet points down, there's an indication that on 25th March NATO started bombing. It's directly above the mention of electricity being turned off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, but I'm talking about the 24th of March. I'm talking about the -- I'm not talking about the 25th because I'm taking it one day at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, you will then have to accept that there is a specific mention of NATO bombing. The date given here is the 25th of March and I understand the witness to be saying that there is some misunderstanding about these particular dates, the 23rd, 24th, and 25th in these notes. With all that premise, then your question may be able to be put.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This is the first note taken when the witness arrived in Macedonia, and I presume that the Tribunal's investigator conscientiously noted what she said, and it corresponds to the statement that she gave on the 13th of June, 2001. And since the note was taken at a time when her memory was the freshest, I referred to it. But let's proceed. If we could put -- bring up the document P00013. I apologise, this is a 65 ter document 00013 map of Pristina that we already saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Madam Bala, could you please encircle the location of your house again.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Before I encircle it, I want to point out again that it's not a detailed map. You cannot see the exact street where I live. So I will orient myself from what I can read here marked as general areas. It should be somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. This map is not detailed at all. Please, could you place number 1 next to it.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And the old green market, where was it located, please?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: From what can I read here, bazaar, it shouldn't be far from this area. So I will orient myself from bazaar here and I will mark it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please put number 2 next to it.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In your statement you said that from the roof-top of your building you observed and saw vehicles with no number plates. Could you please indicate where those vehicles passed.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Just by my house, the house where I live now, the house that I've described earlier, it is situated between two streets, the Llapi Street and the Hoxhe Kadri Prishtina Street. So it's between these two streets, and the movement of these cars or vehicles without registration plates was seen here. Because as soon as a NATO bombing would stop, they would go out and made these uncontrolled movements with their cars and fire in the air and so on and so forth. So there was no need to concentrate on observing things better because you could see them right there, they were pretty close.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How tall is your building?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: It is a five-storey house. Two serve as a cellar or ground floor, and two other floors are used as living space.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Bala. So this would be a two-storey house. Could you please mark where you saw barricades and barbed wire around the town from your roof-top or your terrace.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: What barbed wire? I did not say in my statement that I saw barbed wire from my terrace. I saw the wire -- barbed wire and the police check-points when I travelled by car to different parts of Prishtina, but from my terrace you could not see the barbed wire barricades; from there, you could see the movements of the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you see barbed wire and blockading of Pristina? Where were those points? Could you please indicate them on the map.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: If you're patient, I will explain them one by one. From 20th of March until a day before we were expelled, I will explain where these check-points were. This is a part between Fushe Kosove and Prishtina, this is a part called Ajvali between Prishtina towards Cjivlan --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but I have to interrupt you. You are answering a question that I did not ask. In your 30th June, 2001 statement, last paragraph on page 2 says, On the 26th of March I continued observing the town of VJ and MUP set up blockades which were also secured by barbed wire. This is what I'm asking you about. Where were those blockades and the barbed wire? You're wasting my time and not answering my questions. Could you please mark on the map the check-points and the barbed wire. I'm not asking you anything else but to mark those things on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: This is what I was trying to point out on the map, where these check-points were with barbed wire, with sacks, sand sacks, then blockades with tanks and Pinzgauers. So I was about to mark all of these check-points. Will you allow me to?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is what you marked out here --

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: All of them are marked here because you interrupted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: The main entry and exit points to Prishtina, the part that directly links Prishtina with the road to Mitrovica and Fushe Kosove, then the road to Gjilan, the part where I live, the crossroads at the Nena Center in Prishtina. So these were the areas where these check-points were erected. I will start from -- with the area where I lived. The first crossroads there is by the district court in Prishtina --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, Madam. You marked out where those check-points were. Could you please indicate the road to Kosovska Mitrovica here on the map.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: From the Dragodan area, the road to Mitrovica should be here in this part, the road to Fushe Kosove should be here, on this part here, as -- to the extent I can be oriented on this map. The third circle marks the road to Gjilan. So in other words every entry and exit point from Prishtina was encircled or under siege by the police and military forces. Within the town itself, on the main part of the town, on the main crossroads, there were check-points erected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: To help enable the transcript to understand what has been said, the witness has marked a series of small circles within the map, which she says were each the location of a check-point. She has also marked three large circles on the extremities of the map, one to the left, one to the right, and one at the bottom, and these are the exit points to roadways leading out of the town. Now, if it's going to matter which road leads where in your case, we may have to get those three individually identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: With respect to those large circles, Madam, please indicate and mark the road to Kosovska Mitrovica with the initials KM.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And the road to Kosovo Polje with KP.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And the third circle, I don't know where this road leads to.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you allow me to make a clarification, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to be very clear. It is really difficult for me to orient myself based on this map. So the markings I've made are not accurate. It's exact -- they do not refer to the exact location, it's the approximate location. So these are not 100 per cent accurate markings. I cannot orient myself very good on this map. However, I want to explain and be clear about the check-points that I've seen and verified their existence. There are two -- four main entries to Prishtina, the main entry coming from the direction of Vranjevc, that road takes you to the border with Serbia, to Merdare. There there was a police and army check-point. The next check-point was at the part that links Prishtina with the road to Mitrovica. We call that location Ura e Fushe Kosoves because there is a bridge there where the Prishtina Corps was situated at the time. The military barracks are still there. The next check-point was on the crossroads of the roads to Prishtina and Fushe Kosove. And the next check-point was behind the hospital, we call it "at the circle," which separates the roads going to Prishtina, Kacanik, Gjilan, and to other areas, up to Skopje. There were also check-points within the town itself, inside the town. There are four neighbourhoods or areas of Prishtina: Dragodan, and there the check-point was erected at the bridge of Dragodan; then Vranjevc, there the check-point was at the bridge of Vranjevc; and the technical school, the part where I live and work, there there was a check-point also; then the crossroads between Taslixhe and Germi, there was a check-point there too; and the check-point at the very centre of Prishtina, for identification purposes we call that location "brotherhood monument." So this was the meeting-point of all the convoys of people who had left their homes, who were expelled from their homes, and from that crossroads they were directed towards the train station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that, which I'm sure will help Mr. Djurdjic. You have, dealing with those three big circles outside the map, you've identified two of them. The one on the right-hand side, what is the -- that indicating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole area here, I will try to encircle it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about the one on the other side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one. [Interpretation] Here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yeah. Is that indicating the direction of a roadway to a particular town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see now the areas Aktash, Ulpiana, so it connects with the villages of Mramor, Busi, and so on, and it takes you in the direction of Gjilan. We call it the Karadak part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Now, Mr. Djurdjic, we're going to have to have the second break at about this time. I assume that you'll be finishing today? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would seek shorter answers. I would be finished in 20 minutes' time. If we could keep this map on the screen because we have two more things to mark after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's dangerous. We could lose the lot. It will need to be tendered, but if your questions are shorter and clearer the answers are likely to be shorter and clearer, though a lot of the problem comes from the question, Mr. Djurdjic. We will receive this present map as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00052, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and we resume at five past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Madam Bala, would you please mark again the location of your house on this map we see on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Once again, approximately here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you place number 1 next to it.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you please indicate the exit towards Skopje.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: You want me to mark from my house to that, so this is the main road --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Encircle, by doing so indicating where the exit towards Skopje is.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the road towards Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: This part here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please put a P and the lower circle, please, next to it put SK.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Another thing I'd like to ask you, this red road if you were to travel along it would you reach Skopje next to your circle?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I already said that this is approximate and that it's difficult for me to orient myself on this map. However, this part here is the hospital area which we call the circle of Pristina at the crossroads there, and the road then continues to Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please encircle the exit towards Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, Mitrovica, about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please indicate Vranjavac here on this map, where it's located.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Vranjevc must be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Madam Bala, the road traversing the Vranjavac hill, what is the distance from the summit to the traffic lights close to your house?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: There are no traffic lights close to my house. The traffic lights are close to the centre of the town, right here. There are none close to my house. Two or three streets take you from my house to Vranjevc. From my house to Vranjevc would be a maximum of 1 kilometre. The Llapi mosque is here and that part is linked with Vranjevc.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Madam Bala, do you have to go through the whole of Vranjavac to reach the road leading to Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: You have to go through Vranjevc. Vranjevc is made up of two parts, the upper part and the lower part. The upper part is where the police station was and other houses, while the lower part is the part where the primary school Zenel Hajdini is. The road goes through Vranjevc, to Podujevo, and then to the border with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the distance you have to take through Vranjavac to reach to the summit of the hill and then continue along the road to Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Well, that's a long distance from Vranjevc to Podujevo you mean. Up to Orlane it is 21 kilometres. Orlane is halfway between Vranjevc and Podujevo or so, and from Vranjevc to Podujevo, it's about 60 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm only asking you about the distance between the Vranjavac peak and the bottom of the hill down in Pristina, what is the distance in terms of kilometres?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I don't know and never measured it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Will you agree that it must be at least 3 kilometres between the peak and the bottom of the hill by taking the road?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: As I said earlier, from my house to Vranjevc, that is about 1 kilometre. I don't know how long or how far it is from the other parts of Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what about the distance between Donji Vranjavac and Gornji Vranjavac?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: A road goes through Vranjevc that divides both parts. This is just a small area. You cannot just identify distances by kilometres there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that from the roof that night you saw two APCs heading towards Dragodan. Can you please describe the APCs for me.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: When I was observing from the terrace in the direction of Dragodan, I was observing the area close to the cemetery and I could see the police forces moving in APCs, trucks, and other vehicles. There was a meadow there, a low area, where I could see everything very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mark a number 2 there, please, the location of the APCs.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what do you think would be the distance between your house and what you marked now as number 2?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I don't know the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also say that you saw a tank firing. Can you mark the tank's location, please.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: The tank fired in the day-time. There is a hill in the village Lokare, that's what we call it, and the military base was there. The tank was on top of that hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please put a number 3 there to mark the tank?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about this military base, was it the other side of the hill looking from your house or your side of the hill?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: The military base was behind the hill, I could not see it; but the hill is there, it's a barren hill, rocky hill. It can still be seen from my house, and the tank was on top of that hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now please mark Kojlovci hill.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: The Kolovica area must be somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Put a letter K there.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Taslidj, can you mark that one for me, please.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I'm encircling here the Taslixhe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what about the artillery at Vranjavac that you saw that was firing at Kojlovci hill, can you mark that too.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: It was on the main road that divides the lower and upper Vranjevc, and their movements were along this area. Not only an APC but there were other vehicles moving along that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please mark the location of Hartica house.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: It's close to the main road. I don't know where to mark. As I said, it's close to the main road, about here maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please put an X there.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And we have 1, 2, and 3, can you please put an X there and a number 4.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at your 14th of May [sic], 1999 statement. You said that at Kolovica there was fighting. Who was fighting who, can you tell us that, please?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: There was bombing from the Lukare base, from that hill; the tank was firing against or towards Kolovica against the civilian population and their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I will now read back a portion of your statement to you, the 14th of September [sic], 1999: I saw fighting erupting between the Serbs and the civilians. Many of them started running. The fighting continued for the rest of the day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The statement, Mr. Djurdjic, is the 14th of April, 1999, and that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, the note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- and that is Exhibit D51. It's notes made by another person, not a statement made by and signed by the witness. But you've referred to the 14th of May and the 14th of September. I take it you mean the 14th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] April, yes, the 14th of April. Whenever I say the 14th of April I mean the notes made by the ICTY investigators. The 13th of June statement makes clear that the interview was conducted and a note drawn up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, that's Exhibit D51.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, do you wish --

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: You don't need to ask me for further clarification. That day at midday the tank fired from that hill towards the civilian houses in Kolovica, and that shelling, that firing, for us meant war. The civilian population, unarmed civilian population that were being shelled, left that area and went towards the area where I was living, where my house was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, it reads: "I saw fighting erupting between the Serbs and the population. The fighting continued for the rest of the day." It takes two to have a fight, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: In some parts of Kolovica the fighting occurred during that period, and what I meant by fighting was not fighting between two equal parts or sides but the firing from one side onto another side, which was the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Bala, would I be right to say that no members of your family had their documents seized at the border?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, because there was no time and no space. We did not have the documentation or the IDs on us when we left for the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Bala, what about all of the persons passing through check-points, were they not all checked and inspected?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: If they had decided to check all the people who went through those check-points, it would take months -- it would have taken months. They only picked out certain people that were separated from their families, they were looted and beaten, but not everybody on the convoy were -- was checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You tell us today that a Yugoslav army officer entered your house, and then when the next group came along it included Ivica a man you knew from before as a police officer. Ms. Bala, in the 14th of April note, the only thing you state is that a member of the Army of Yugoslavia came in as well as a Roma man. In your 13th of June, 2001, statement you state that a member of the Yugoslav army came and a Romani man. How come you only remembered today to share with us the fact that this Roma person was a police officer and was a member of that first group and not the other one?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I said the same thing then, and I will repeat it again. They were in a group. When I say "they," these were policemen and other people who were mobilised. When they came to the houses, they each went to a different house --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, let's keep this as short as possible. You've answered my question, and I will now put to you your own statement dated the 13th of June, 2001. This is paragraph 11 where you say: "On the 29th of March VJ, MUP, Serb civilians, and gypsies wearing police uniforms continued to go into Albanian houses and forcing the residents to leave. I was still observing this from my terrace -- I was still observing this from my terrace. Later that day the VJ officer and a gypsy came to our house." Ms. Bala, no mention there of the traffic policeman, no naming him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, it may save us a lot of time if I point out that in the supplementary statement of the witness, Exhibit 421, the witness at paragraph 10 says that: "The gypsy that I referred to I know by the name of Ivica. He was a traffic police officer before March 1999 and operated in our neighbourhood." So I think you need to take that into account when you're putting the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm taking into account the fact that that was a 2006 statement, and the one I'm talking about is a 2001 statement. Likewise, we have the April note from 1999, where we find no mention of the name or indeed the official capacity of that person, the Roma person. It wasn't before 2006 that the traffic policeman was mentioned and named, and that is why I'm asking the witness this particular question. How come in 2006 all of a sudden she knows this, something that she didn't know back in 2001 or indeed back in 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can clarify. When I was asked to identify who that person was, I did give the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that upon entering Kosovo Polje you saw some bodies lying on the ground. How could you tell their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Well, considering the fact that Fushe Kosove had been burned, destroyed, razed to the ground, and emptied of the Albanian population, the bodies that were on the street were half burnt or burnt bodies; and later on people identified them as Albanian victims. The police and army forces were on both sides of the road or the street, and they could see the bodies lying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, would I be right to say that you did not see the way in which those persons came to grief?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Well, there was such destruction in Fushe Kosove, that's what led me to assume that they were Albanian victims; however, I was not there when that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I want to know is about you walking along the rail track from Djeneral Jankovic to Blace. Blace is in Macedonia, can you confirm that for me, please.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: It's a neutral area between Kosova and Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on in order to avoid wasting time. There is a border there. A town is always either side of the border, not in between. Can you tell me whether the policemen and officers at any point followed you as you were walking along the railway track?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: We went to Hani i Elezet, close to the cement factory, and there we found police and army forces with their barrels pointed towards us. They started to check for IDs, but then they stopped, and they forced us to walk two by two on that rail track.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You are not answering my question, are you? My question was: Did the police provide security for you, did they escort you, while you were walking along the railway track? That is the gist of my question. Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Your question is not clear to me; however, I will try to answer it. As I said, the forces were there expecting us, and we were ordered to form lines, to walk along -- between the tracks and not to go outside the tracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: My question is: Were policemen or soldiers or both groups following you or escorting you as you were walking down the railway track?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: No, they were not escorting us because both sides of the rail track were mined. If they had escorted us they would have been blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do have a couple of questions left, but I'm ready to drop them because I think it would be fair to leave the OTP some time to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you wanting to tender this further map? We'll get you a piece of red string to put on your finger.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I think that would probably be the best solution. Yes, please, I would like to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00053, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Behar, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, just very briefly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, you were asked some questions about the location of the railway station and then particular question from His Honour. Can I ask you: Do you remember what you passed as you walked with the convoy on the way to the train station?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Well, I'll mention them one by one. From Llapi Street, where I live, we went to Proleteri Street, then from Proleteri Street to the main street, to the brotherhood square. From this square we went towards the train station or the Dragodan road. We reached the Dragodan bridge, and from there the train station is not very far away so we went from there to the train station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And just so I'm clear then, does that mean -- did you go through the centre en route?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: The brotherhood and unity square, there is a monument there, that is the centre of Prishtina. We went through the centre. However, there were other convoys coming from all corners of Prishtina that were joining the main convoy, going through the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And my final question is just with respect to a question you were asked by counsel for Mr. Djordjevic. He asked you why you'd never mentioned seeing masks or painted faces before in any of your statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can we have the witness's addendum up on the screen, it was marked as P00420. We'll need the addendum and page 2 of the addendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: There.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Just drawing your attention then to paragraph 9, about line 5, again this is from your addendum taken in 2006. Can you just read that line out loud for us.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: [In English] I have to read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If you could read it aloud for us, and I'll just ask you a very brief question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you prefer it in Albanian, which is coming up now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: There's a line there that references painted faces. If you could read that aloud. You can take a moment to find it.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: I don't have it not yet now in Albanian, but I will continue in English to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Okay. If that's fine. I know you do speak English.

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Yeah, I do. Thank you. "I was able to distinguish the police from VJ by their uniforms. The VJ," that means Vojska Jugoslavije, "had green uniforms, the police blue. Badges or patches worn on the uniforms would have Yugoslav Army and MUP," that means Ministarstvo Unutrasnjih Poslova, "in Serbian, written on them. Additionally, the police tended to have police, again in Serbian, written on the back of the uniforms. The only forces that I was unable to distinguish were the person who dressed all in black. They wore no patches on their clothing. They wore masks or have painted faces and they would wear scarves on the head and arms" --

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: That's fine. I'll just stop you there. Does that help you to remember whether or not you had mentioned this before in a previous statement?

utterances.speaker: NAZALIE BALA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Those are my questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'll be pleased to know, Ms. Bala, that that concludes the questions for you. We've just finished in time for the day, fortunately. The Chamber would like to thank you for coming again to The Hague and for the assistance that you have been able to give, and you may now, of course, now return to your ordinary activities. And when we rise, the court officer will show you out. So once again, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We resume tomorrow in the afternoon at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 17th day of March, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.
